I haven't been sourcing in weeks. For one thing, my bike was stolen at the end of September and I've only just replaced it. For another, my inventory was already overflowing and I had to prune the books I felt least likely to sell: hardcovers, new books, and books in unsaleable condition. Finally, I was saving up proceeds for other investments in my business than inventory, which surprises I can hopefully spring on my readers soon.

[Subscribe now](https://sillywackyzanybooks.substack.com/subscribe?){.button .primary}

But the dominoes began to fall! I have made my investments, offloaded by undesirable books, and my new bike arrived, an Aventon Abound I have christened the Bookmobike II.

So Friday morning I was back in the saddle. I got to the house on Seabury Avenue at 8:30 in the morning. The doors were to open at 10:00. When you arrive before doors open on the first day of an estate sale, you take a number from the organizers, and customers enter the sale in the order of their number. Usually the organizers hand out their numbers from 30 to 90 minutes before the doors open, but the most committed attendees will be there well before that time. The community provides their own solution, which are called pre-numbers. Regulars who expect to arrive first will bring a pad of post-it notes, write down numbers on each one, and hang it from a ziploc bag on the outside of their car for attendees to take as they arrive. Almost every estate sale company honors pre-numbers, and some - like the company organizing this sale - forgo handing out their own numbers and rely on pre-numbers exclusively. 90 minutes before doors, I was number 23.

I had my eyes on something specific, something that had been highlighted in the listing. In my experience, when something is singled out in the listing, it's because the company knows it's valuable and is going to charge retail (or even higher!). They use it to lure you in the door. You cluck your tongue and shake your head at the price on the item, but hey - you're here, you might as well take a look around. I knew that was a possibility. I also knew that, even if it were reasonably priced, its desirability and prominence in the listing meant that I would be competing for it with other customers. There aren't that many book buyers in my area - a couple of bookstore owners, a collector, a few barcode scanner scouts. None of these people specialize in vintage paperbacks like I do, but these are also particularly famous and collectible books. I was nervous.

Waiting in line, I struck up a conversation with a cute clothing reseller, and just as the organizers started calling us in one at a time, she surreptitiously handed me number 18 - she had taken two numbers, but her friend never showed up. We went in together but quickly parted: the clothing she was after was in a second-floor bedroom, but books were scattered throughout the house. The photograph from the listing showed what I was looking for on a plain wooden table, and it had probably been put back in its proper place after the photo was taken. The dining room table was covered in paperbacks: CS Lewis suggested I was on the right trail, but I could not see what I desired. I powerwalked the length and breadth and heighth of the house like Scott Pilgrim looking for Ramona Flowers, but still my quarry eluded me. My heart sank. Someone had snatched them up so quickly I never saw them.

I took one more chance: I opened the picture of the item on my phone and asked the organizer is she knew where pictured items were. She said if they hadn't sold, they'd be back on the shelves in the library on the second floor. The room bristled with people, with the beeping of scanners and dull thud of books being tumbled into Bankers Boxes indiscriminately. They could not possibly remain. I checked the shelves, which seemed relatively unmolested, but did not have what I wanted. I cast my eyes down, and while I stood there trying to come to terms with my defeat, something in the back of my brain was trying to grab my attention. My eyes had seen something - what?

Paydirt. On the floor were three cardboard palettes of books, stacked one on top of another. The topmost one was askew, and revealed the spines of the last few books in the row beneath it. And there they were, the books from the listing. \$2 each.

*The Two Towers* and *The Return of the King* are in the beautiful pirate Ace edition, published without permission or royalty when the copyright of *The Lord of the Rings* was not firmly established in the US. Tolkien's publisher had to bribe Ace to stop printing them, and run their own Ballantine paperbacks, with minor textual revisions to get the copyright sorted out, that famously bore the legend THE AUTHORIZED EDITION OF THE FAMOUS FANTASY TRILOGY. Tolkien didn't think much of the baffling Ballantine cover art, and he certainly didn't like calling *The Lord of the Rings* a trilogy, but he was so incensed about the Ace editions that he didn't put up too much of a fuss.

*Star of the Unborn* is a German science fiction novel that has been forgotten twice: once after its publication in 1946, and again after its publication by Ballantine in 1976 as a "rediscovered masterpiece." It has now been rediscovered again by [Matt from Bookpilled](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D0McEPWvT3A&pp=ygUdYm9va3BpbGxlZCBzdGFyIG9mIHRoZSB1bmJvcm4%3D), and after his review, these 1976 Ballantines became highly sought after. It is still possible to find them on the shelves of bookstores that priced them before the value changed, which is how I got my first copy. This copy will be for sale.

Giddy and perhaps even shaking, I tossed them into my grocery bag like I was getting away with something. I stood up straight and allowed my muscles to relax. I could finally start looking at all the rest of the books.

I probably only spent about ten more minutes there. Here's what I picked up:
